claims.text: The initial FeNiCrCoCu coating on a Cu matrix has an FCC structure.
The FeNiCrCoCu coating has stable wear resistance at 300 K.
The FeNiCrCoCu coating has a high elastic modulus at 300 K.
A transition from stable to unstable wear occurs at approximately 400–500 K.
Below approximately 400–500 K, low stacking-fault energy promotes wide stacking faults and stable dislocation structures.
Stable stacking faults and dislocation structures maintain wear resistance and high elastic modulus below the threshold.
Increasing temperature reduces the stacking-fault energy of FeNiCrCoCu.
Plastic deformation shifts from dislocation glide to dislocation climb as temperature increases.
At low temperature, high stacking-fault energy stabilizes dislocation glide and stacking faults.
Glide and stacking-fault stabilization enable work hardening and wear resistance.
Reduced stacking-fault energy promotes dislocation cross-slip.
Elevated temperature facilitates stress-assisted dislocation climb controlled by lattice diffusion.
Low stacking-fault energy promotes dynamic recrystallization.
Dynamic recrystallization produces grain refinement and increases the opportunity for grain-boundary sliding.
Cross-slip, climb, and dynamic recrystallization cause rapid lattice disorder and lattice softening.
Lattice disorder, grain refinement, and softening reduce load-bearing capacity and cause wear instability.
Above approximately 400–500 K, wear resistance and elastic modulus decline sharply.
The high-temperature transition is accompanied by increased dislocation density and tangled dislocation substructures.
The high-temperature transition is accompanied by dynamic recrystallization.
The critical temperature depends on alloy chemistry, grain size, strain rate, processing history, and testing conditions.

contradictions.description: The hypothesis says that low SFE below the threshold stabilizes wide stacking faults and dislocation structures, whereas the mechanism says that high SFE at low temperature stabilizes glide and stacking faults.

Reduced SFE is invoked both to stabilize wide stacking faults below the threshold and, after further reduction, to promote cross-slip above the threshold, without explaining how the same trend produces these opposing regimes.
